hints: Use the work-energy principle: the loss in gravitational potential energy equals the gain in kinetic energy plus the work done against air resistance.
Calculate the loss in gravitational potential energy $mgh = 1.6(10)(9)$ and the gain in kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{1}{2}(1.6)(12)^2$.
Subtract the kinetic energy from the potential energy to find the work done against air resistance.
walkthrough:
Calculate the loss in gravitational potential energy as the particle falls 9 m:
$$\Delta E_p = mgh = 1.6 \times 10 \times 9 = 144\text{ J}$$

Calculate the gain in kinetic energy from rest to $12\text{ m s}^{-1}$:
$$\Delta E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{1}{2}(1.6)(12)^2 = 0.8 \times 144 = 115.2\text{ J}$$

Apply the work-energy principle to determine the work done against air resistance:
$$W_{\text{resistance}} = \Delta E_p - \Delta E_k = 144 - 115.2 = 28.8\text{ J}$$

teacher_walkthrough:
Name the foundational principle: the work-energy theorem states that the loss in mechanical energy equals the work done against opposing non-conservative forces such as air resistance:
$$W_{\text{resistance}} = \Delta E_p - \Delta E_k$$

Calculate the gravitational potential energy lost by the $1.6\text{ kg}$ particle falling from a height of $9\text{ m}$:
$$\Delta E_p = mgh = (1.6)(10)(9)$$
$$1.6 \times 10 = 16$$
$$\Delta E_p = 16 \times 9 = 144\text{ J}$$

Calculate the kinetic energy gained by the particle from rest ($u = 0\text{ m s}^{-1}$) to its landing speed $v = 12\text{ m s}^{-1}$:
$$\Delta E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{1}{2}(1.6)(12)^2$$
$$12^2 = 144$$
$$\frac{1}{2} \times 1.6 = 0.8$$
$$\Delta E_k = 0.8 \times 144 = 115.2\text{ J}$$

Subtract the kinetic energy gained from the potential energy lost to find the work done against air resistance:
$$W_{\text{resistance}} = 144 - 115.2 = 28.8\text{ J}$$
